 MySA Logo Newsletters SOUND OFF: Have you encountered any issues or inconsistencies while voting in the S.A. area? San Antonio News Texas Social Security checks are going up in 2027. Could cuts be on the way?
 A U.S. senator warns the program's trust fund is running low and the 2027 COLA could accelerate its depletion.
 By Melanie Love Salazar , Digital Trending Reporter Oct 21, 2026 After the Social Security COLA 2027 announcement of 3.6%, Louisiana Senator Bill Cassidy warns it may quicken the depletion of the program's trust fund.
 Veronique D/Courtesy of Getty Images Texas retirees were finally briefed on Social Security's 2027 cost-of-living adjustment (COLA) this month. The administration announced a 3.6% increase in benefits, but one public official argues it could cause major issues in the near future.
 Social Security Administration COLA increase
 In a press release issued Wednesday, October 14, the Social Security Administration (SSA) said that, on average, retirement payments will increase by $75 per month. This aligns with past projections from the AARP , a nonprofit serving Americans ages 50 and up, as previously reported by MySA . 
 Advertisement
 Article continues below this ad
 Benefits include Old-Age, Survivors, and Disability Insurance (OASDI) and Supplemental Security Income (SSI). Over 70 million beneficiaries belong to these groups. 
 Social Security trust fund depletion
 The purpose of COLA is to help recipients afford roughly the same amount of products and services during periods of higher costs. SSA Commissioner Frank J. Bisignano previously described it as a way to ensure "benefits reflect today’s economic realities and continue to provide a foundation of security."

However, in an interview with FOX Business released the same day as the COLA announcement, Louisiana Senator Bill Cassidy (R) alleged that, because the number is so much higher, it's going to drain the program's trust fund much faster. At the same time, he acknowledged that the amount does reflect recent inflation. 
 Advertisement
 Article continues below this ad
 "So, if we now have, like, 5.5 years until the trust fund goes empty, at which point, by law, there'll be a 28.5% benefit cut, or Congress ignores the law and just starts to borrow money like crazy to pay benefits," Cassidy said. "The clock is ticking."
 The SSA has said that findings from the 2026 Trustees of the Social Security and Medicare reports revealed that trust funds for the Old-Age and Survivors Insurance (OASI) and Hospital Insurance (HI) "will be able to pay 100 percent of total scheduled benefits until at least 2032" before the funds’ reserves are depleted. 
 At that point, continuing program income would be sufficient to cover 78% (OASI) or 89% (HI) of total scheduled benefits, according to the SSA website . 
 In the past, Cassidy has proposed that the federal government borrow $1.5 trillion and place it in a separate investment fund to offset this, "guaranteeing that whatever the Social Security recipient is scheduled to receive, they continue to receive," per a press release . 
 Advertisement
 Article continues below this ad
 "This separate fund, accruing returns over 70 years with a diversified investment portfolio and strong guardrails, addresses the majority of the Social Security shortfall," Cassidy said during a keynote speech at the National Institute on Retirement Security’s 15th Annual Retirement Policy Conference. 
 According to the SSA, Social Security beneficiaries will start to see higher checks in January 2027. Those receiving SSI payments will start receiving increases on December 31, 2026. 
 Oct 21, 2026 Melanie Love Salazar Digital Trending Reporter Melanie Love Salazar is a digital trending reporter for MySA who is passionate about telling stories that inspire, uplift, and inform readers. She was born and raised in San Antonio and is currently based near Austin. She specializes in covering music, culture, and trending news, but loves any opportunity to talk about fandom and digital media.
Melanie graduated from Texas State University with a BS in journalism and a minor in creative writing. She is currently pursuing a master's degree in American Journalism through New York University.
